title: How to make tutorial videos people actually finish
summary: How to make tutorial videos step by step: pick one task, record first, script from the recording, and keep every video current as your product changes
body_markdown:
Most advice on tutorial videos says to keep them under 90 seconds. We looked at the 87,267 videos teams exported from Clueso over the past year, and 61% of them run longer than that. The median lands just under two minutes, and a third go past three.


The teams making those videos aren't ignoring the advice. They're making each video as long as its task. This guide walks through how to make a tutorial video that way, from choosing the task to keeping the video accurate after your product changes.


## What is a tutorial video?


A tutorial video is a short recording that shows a viewer how to complete one specific task, usually on screen, with narration explaining each step and why it matters. It differs from a demo or an explainer because the viewer is expected to repeat the task, often with the video paused next to the product.


For software, that means the real interface. The viewer needs to see the button labels and the account state they'll actually have, because a near-miss teaches them to distrust the rest of your library.


## How do you make a tutorial video, step by step?


Most guides start with a script and then record the screen to match it. Every surprise in the product sends you back to rewrite, and your subject-matter expert ends up performing clicks in time with a voice. Recording first gives you the ground truth, and the script follows from it.


### 1. Name one task and the outcome


Write the task the way a viewer would search for it: "How to export a report to CSV," not "Reporting overview." If you can't state the finished outcome in one sentence, you have two videos. A title with "overview" in it usually means the video covers several tasks.


### 2. Set up the account before you record


Use a demo account with realistic data, close your notifications, and raise the app's zoom level so text survives compression. Anything you'd have to blur later is cheaper to remove now. Then check that your starting state matches the viewer's. If a new customer's account won't have sample projects, yours shouldn't either.


### 3. Record the workflow and talk through it roughly


Do the task once at normal speed and narrate as you go, fumbles included. Nobody will hear this audio. It exists so you have a transcript of what you did and said, in the order the product made you do it, and you'll fix the words in the next step. Our guide to[recording clean screen videos](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-make-tasteful-screen-capture-videos) covers the recording craft in detail.


### 4. Write the script from the recording


Clean the transcript into a script. Cut the filler, name every click specifically ("select Reports, then Export"), and open with one sentence on what the task gets the viewer. Without it, the viewer follows six clicks without knowing what they're for. A script written this way matches the product step for step, because the product wrote its first draft.


### 5. Replace the voice and direct attention


Rough narration needs to become a clean voiceover, and the viewer's eye needs to land on the right part of the screen at each step. You can do this with a separate editor and a text-to-speech tool, moving files between them.


At Clueso, the recording's transcript becomes the script,[filler words and silences come out](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-cuts) , and your audio is replaced with an[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) .[Zooms and callouts](https://www.clueso.io/features/visual-effects) land on the real interface, and the same recording produces a[written step-by-step guide](https://www.clueso.io/features/help-articles) .


> Teamworks' customer education team[cut production from 4–5 hours to 20–30 minutes a video](https://www.clueso.io/customers/teamworks) working this way.


### 6. Cut to the task, not to a target length


Watch the export once as a first-time viewer would. Trim the dead air where the product loads, and end the moment the outcome appears on screen. If the video still feels long, check whether it's really one task. Split it rather than speeding it up.


### 7. Publish the written version next to the video


Some viewers want to watch. Others want to skim the steps with the product open in another tab. Put the video and a step-by-step article on the same help center page, and give the video a title that matches the phrase people search. If you're starting from existing articles instead, here's how to[turn a help article into a short walkthrough video](https://www.clueso.io/blog/help-article-to-walkthrough-video) .


## How long should a tutorial video be?


A tutorial should run as long as its task takes. Across the exports in our data, the middle half of videos run between about one minute and three and a half minutes (63 to 217 seconds), and 32% run past three minutes.


Those longer videos aren't necessarily failures. A setup workflow with eight screens takes longer than toggling a setting, and cutting it to 90 seconds means dropping a step the viewer needed. The better test is whether a video covers more than one outcome. If your script contains a second "now let's…", that's where the next video starts.


## Which type of tutorial video do you need?


Start from what the viewer needs to do, and the format follows from it. The same screen recording can become a feature announcement or a support answer depending on where it's placed and what it opens with.


What the viewer needs


Tutorial type


Where it lives


Adopt a new feature


[Outcome-first walkthrough](https://www.clueso.io/blog/product-walkthrough-videos) : why it matters, then the clicks


Changelog, in-app announcement, release email


Fix a problem without filing a ticket


How-to video paired with a written article


Help center, support macros, chatbot answers


Get set up in their first week


[A sequence of short videos](https://www.clueso.io/blog/customer-onboarding-videos) , one per setup task


Onboarding checklist, welcome emails


Learn an internal tool or process


Modular videos, one per workflow


Wiki, LMS, SOP pages


Learn in their own language


The same tutorial with translated voiceover, captions, and on-screen text


Localized help center


The last row is where most libraries stall, because translating a tutorial by hand means recording it again in every language. Our guide to[translating training and product videos](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-translate-a-video) covers what to localize and in what order.


## How do you keep software tutorial videos up to date?


Software tutorials go out of date on a schedule you don't control. A release that renames one button breaks every video that shows it. In our data, 29% of videos were exported more than once and 12% three times or more, so a large share of published tutorials get reopened after they ship.


Keeping one task per video is what makes those updates cheap. A renamed button then touches one short video instead of a ten-minute overview, and a script-driven video can be regenerated after a wording change without re-recording. The other habit worth building is a simple log of which screens each video shows, so when a release note lands you can find the affected videos in minutes rather than rewatching the library. We've written a longer guide to[keeping a training video library current](https://www.clueso.io/blog/training-video-library) .


## How do you know if a tutorial video worked?


A view count tells you someone found the video, not whether they finished the task. The signals that matter are whether viewers take the action the video teaches, and whether support tickets on that topic drop after you publish.


CloudEagle saw[product how-to support ticket volume fall by 60%](https://www.clueso.io/customers/cloudeagle) after building out its help videos and documentation. Teamworks tracks course completion against what people actually do in the product afterwards. The cheapest version of either test is a ticket search: pick one tutorial, and count how-to tickets on its topic for the month before it went live and the month after.


## Frequently asked questions


### How can video tutorials improve product adoption for complex features?


Break the feature into the tasks a user actually performs, and make one short video per task. Place each one where the user meets the feature, in the release note, the empty state, or the help article. The setup video usually matters most, because nobody reaches the advanced steps without it.


### What should a SaaS video tutorial include for user adoption?


One task, one sentence on why it matters, and the real interface with each click called out. End on a state the viewer can check against their own screen, and pair the video with a written version for people who'd rather read.


### How do you make effective SaaS onboarding video tutorials?


Map the first few tasks a new user must complete to get value, and make one short video per task in the order they happen. Put them in the onboarding checklist instead of a video library, so each one appears when the user needs it. There's more on sequencing in our[SaaS customer onboarding guide](https://www.clueso.io/blog/saas-customer-onboarding) .


### Is there a way to let customers search video tutorials and jump to specific answers?


Yes. Publish each video with a transcript and a written step-by-step version on the same page, and add chapters to anything longer than a couple of minutes. Search then indexes the text, and viewers can jump to the step they need instead of scrubbing through the video.


---


Before you record anything, open last month's support tickets and pull every one that starts with "how do I." Each one is a tutorial video with its title already written. Make the most frequent one this week, then count how-to tickets on that topic for the next 30 days.
